coverageDimensions:
SERVICE coverage — this is the only dimension the page actually supplies, and it supplies it completely. Denominator 440 service entries, numerator the Yes count in whichever column you are measuring (or Yes+Partial, stated separately, never blended). One caveat that will bite any join: the 440 rows are IAM's own service-entry granularity, not the AWS service catalogue as marketed. Console features (AWS Activate Console, AWS Action Recommendations), API surfaces (Apache Kafka APIs for Amazon MSK clusters, AWS Tiros API), and versioned variants (API Gateway Management V2, SES v2) each get their own row. So 440 is the correct denominator for a claim about this page, and the wrong denominator for a claim about "AWS services" sourced from a Region table or the Service Authorization Reference. Do not divide one list's numerator by the other's denominator.

REGION coverage — the page gives you nothing. Not one Region name, Region code, partition, or availability statement appears anywhere in the 620 lines. Every one of these claims is global-by-silence. If a coverage map needs a Region dimension for IAM features, it must come from another page; any Region figure attributed to this one is fabricated.

RESOURCE TYPE coverage — the page gives you almost nothing, and this is where a parser is most likely to over-claim, because two column names contain the word "resource". Neither Resource-level permissions nor Resource-based policies enumerates a single resource type; both assert a per-service boolean-ish value and explicitly defer the resource detail elsewhere (the ABAC legend to the condition-key docs, the Actions legend to Actions, Resources, and Condition Keys for AWS Services). The only resource types named anywhere on the page are illustrative fragments inside footnotes covering 27 of 440 rows — Lambda functions, event source mappings and code signing configurations with layers excluded; S3 directory buckets, object resources, Storage Lens, Storage Lens groups and access points; CloudTrail event data stores, dashboards and channels; the IAM role trust policy; X-Ray groups and sampling rules; VPC endpoints; MSK clusters. Those are open-ended examples, not a closed universe, and they exist for 6 percent of rows. There is no denominator, so there is no ratio. Record them, if at all, as prose qualifiers on the Partial values they explain, and get real resource-type coverage from the Service Authorization Reference instead.

features.collapse: The 440 rows are IAM's own service entries, not AWS services. AWS gives one service several rows: Billing has nine, Connect seven, CloudWatch seven, EC2 four. Resolving every row against the service universe — by name, and by the guide each row links to when the name is not one we hold — leaves 327 distinct services and 11 rows that name no service we can identify. 440 is the right denominator for a claim about this page and the wrong one for a claim about AWS services, which is the warning this expectation already carries under coverageDimensions. Where those rows disagree with each other, and 44 of the 52 repeated services do, the merged claim is partial rather than whichever row was read first.
features.reasoning: The bullet legend defines this column as: you can specify individual actions in a policy for this service; if not, you must use * in the Action element. That is 'capability X reaches service Y', enumerated over the 440 rows. The axis is the service, not the action — the page never lists a single action name, and the actual action universe is explicitly deferred to the Service Authorization Reference.
features.scope: None. The only second dimension on this page is the capability column, and that split is already the feature split.

features.statuses: 350 Yes, 76 No, 14 Partial; 350+76+14=440. Not-supported is stated by an explicit No cell (icon-no.png + the word No), not by omission — there are no blank cells. Partial is a distinct third state that AWS defines in the legend ('If a service supports this feature for some resources but not others, it is indicated by Partial'), and 6 of the 14 Partials link to a footnote (AWS Config, Amazon ECS, Amazon Lightsail, Amazon SES v2, AWS Trusted Advisor, AWS X-Ray). Collapsing Partial into Yes overstates coverage by 14 services; collapsing it into No understates by 14.

features.reasoning: The legend defines this as: you can attach resource-based policies to a resource within the service, with a Principal element. The unit of claim is the service. This is the highest-value column for a security coverage map, because resource-based policies are the cross-account trust surface, and it is also the column most distorted by treating Partial as Yes.
features.scope: None. Footnote prose narrows individual rows but states no repeatable second dimension.
features.statuses: 35 Yes, 397 No, 8 Partial; 35+397+8=440. This is the column where exclusions dominate — 397 explicit No cells. Three cells that read Yes or No also carry an (Info) footnote link, so the presence of a footnote does not imply Partial and must not be used to infer the state. Footnotes narrow several Yes/Partial values sharply: IAM supports only the role trust policy; Rekognition only for copying Custom Labels models; Redshift Serverless only to share snapshots; VPC only a single policy on a VPC endpoint; MSK only a cluster policy on a multi-VPC-connectivity cluster.

features.reasoning: The claim is 'this service supports tag-based authorization', made once per service row. Axis is the service. Note the two-level structure AWS has hidden inside one cell: a Yes is itself an assertion over three condition keys and over all of that service's resource types. Do not try to recover either sub-axis from this page — neither is enumerated.
features.scope: None stated as a column. AWS names three condition keys in the legend, and the Multi-party approval footnote is the only place a per-resource split is spelled out (all three keys for identity sources and approval teams; only aws:ResourceTag for sessions). One footnote is not a dimension.
features.statuses: 285 Yes, 136 No, 19 Partial; 285+136+19=440. The table header is the bare word ABAC; the legend bullet gives the full name. AWS defines the tri-state precisely here: Yes means all three condition keys (aws:ResourceTag, aws:RequestTag, aws:TagKeys) for every resource type; Partial means all three keys for only some resource types. So Partial is a resource-type-scoped qualifier expressed without listing the resource types. 7 of the 19 Partials link to footnotes (CodeBuild, IAM, Lambda, Lightsail, Multi-party approval, Amazon S3, AWS X-Ray).

features.reasoning: The legend defines a service-linked role as a role that gives the service permission to act on your behalf, and the Yes/No/Partial is asserted once per service. Axis is the service. This is a genuine security-relevant capability column and is the second-most-populated source of No values on the page.

features.statuses: 150 Yes, 279 No, 11 Partial; 150+279+11=440. Most Yes cells wrap the word Yes in a link to that service's own service-linked-role documentation — the link is decoration on the value, not a different value. 279 explicit No cells. AWS also warns in the legend that this column does not indicate whether the service uses standard service roles, so a No here is not 'no service role'. Footnotes qualify several: CloudWatch (console cannot create them; Alarm Actions only), MediaPackage (access logs only), EC2 (four named features only), Lambda (none, but Lambda@Edge has them), SageMaker AI (Studio and training jobs only), S3 (Storage Lens only).

pageTitle: AWS services that work with IAM
shouldNotExtract: The 10-bullet legend at the top (Service, Actions, Resource-level permissions, Resource-based policies, ABAC, Temporary credentials, Service-linked roles, More information) — that is the column dictionary, not seven capabilities-with-values and not a list of covered things. The 26 H3 headings under "More information" — they are footnote sections attached to 27 table rows, not 26 additional services and not a separate capability list; a parser that harvests H3s will invent a phantom 26-value axis. The "See also" section, whose entire body is the AI-coding-assistant boilerplate bullet about `aws agent-toolkit search-skills` — it is not a capability, a service, or a value. Every icon image URL (icon-yes.png / icon-no.png / icon-maybe.png) — read the adjacent word, and never let the image count as a cell. Every documentation hyperlink, in the Service column and wrapped around Yes/Partial values — link targets are references, not axis values, and the mix of relative .md and absolute https targets is meaningless here. No quotas, pricing, prerequisites, code examples, or troubleshooting appear on this page at all.
trap: The dominant trap is binarising the table: this is a tri-state matrix, and Partial is a first-class value AWS defines twice in the legend. Coercing Partial to Yes inflates coverage by 14 / 8 / 19 / 5 / 11 services across the five meaningful columns; coercing it to No deflates it by the same. Four close seconds. (1) Reading the page as one capability and emitting 440 "works with IAM" claims — the page has six columns and therefore six separate capabilities with genuinely different distributions (Resource-based policies is 35 Yes; Temporary credentials is 429 Yes). (2) Parsing the value from the icon filename instead of the word, which quietly maps icon-maybe.png to whatever the parser guesses; and treating the presence of an (Info) footnote link as meaning Partial, when 3 cells that read Yes or No also carry one. (3) Regex link-stripping: AWS's own Markdown is malformed in 7 cells, which serialise as `Partial ([Info)](url)` with the brackets crossed. A naive `\[([^\]]*)\]\([^)]*\)` substitution yields garbage instead of "Partial", so those rows get dropped or mis-stated. Match the leading word Yes/No/Partial, do not try to parse the link. (4) Row identity: several names contain a non-breaking space (Route 53, Route 53 Domains) which breaks exact-match joins against any other list, and near-duplicate rows are distinct entries that must not be merged — AWS App Mesh vs AWS App Mesh Preview, Amazon API Gateway vs API Gateway Management vs API Gateway Management V2, Amazon SES vs SES v2. "Preview" in a row name is part of the service name, not a lifecycle status; nothing on this page is marked retired or deprecated.
whatThePageStates: This page is a single alphabetical matrix under the heading "Services that work with IAM": 440 data rows, one per AWS service entry as IAM names it, against six IAM feature columns — Actions, Resource-level permissions, Resource-based policies, ABAC, Temporary credentials, Service-linked roles. Each cell is a tri-state value (Yes / No / Partial) rendered as an icon image plus the literal word, so every column is an independent, fully-populated support claim over the same 440-value axis. A "More information" section holds 26 named footnote sections that qualify 27 of the rows in prose (what "Partial" means for that service, or which sub-feature the Yes covers); a "See also" section holds nothing but the AI-coding-assistant boilerplate bullet.
